summary: Lists requirements for Emergency Telecommunication Service (ETS) in the context of IP telephony. It extends the general requirements in RFC 3689 and presents no solutions. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This applies the emergency-call wish list to Internet phones. It says what the system must do so urgent calls from officials can get through, but not how.

questions: what is ets in ip telephony
subtitle: A short wish list for what IP phone systems must support so emergency calls can be recognised and given better service.

tldr.problem: Emergency telecommunication standards exist in other networks, such as labels in SS7 phone networks. Calls that cross between IP telephony and those networks need agreed requirements so the emergency marking survives the trip.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists five requirements for IP telephony signaling: carry extensible labels, map them to labels used in other networks, allow accounting, and support a 'best available' service for labelled traffic. It gives no solutions.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document. It does not mandate anything, and it leaves the design of actual protocols to later documents.

today: RFC 3690 is an Informational RFC, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines requirements only and specifies no protocol; it builds on RFC 3689.

sections.title: Why Emergency Calls Need Requirements
sections.content:
After disasters such as hurricanes, floods, earthquakes and terrorist attacks, recovery work needs immediate access to whatever public telecommunications are at hand. The RFC lists conventional telephones, cellular phones, and Internet access through online terminals, IP telephones and wireless PDAs. Because commercial telecommunications is moving to Internet-based technology, the Internet community needs to think about how to support emergency management.

Other standards bodies have already defined emergency indicators. For example, T1.631 defines specific indicators or labels for emergency communications in Signaling System 7 (SS7) networks. To work across hybrid networks, which connect IP to other networks such as the Public Switched Telephone Network, requirements must be defined so that services can interwork.
sections.eli5: Emergency calls already have special markings on the old phone network. The Internet needs rules so those markings are not lost when a call moves between the two.

sections.title: Scope and What Is Not Required
sections.content:
This document extends the general Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS) requirements in RFC 3689 to the specific case of IP telephony, viewed as an end-to-end application layer service. It does not define solutions, protocol enhancements or specifications. It also notes that RFC 3487, the resource priority requirements for SIP, overlaps with it but applies only to SIP.

The RFC does not mandate that anyone accept the requirements. The IETF does not mandate capabilities for the independent networks that make up the Internet, so an ISP may choose not to run telephony gateways or services at all. The RFC expects that business contracts such as Service Level Agreements will be used for requirements that apply to service providers, and that without an SLA only best effort service is provided. The requirements do not apply to ISPs that choose not to offer ETS.
sections.eli5: The list is advice, not a law. A company that does not offer emergency phone service does not have to follow it.

sections.title: The Five IP Telephony Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements cover only telephony signaling, and explicitly not IP-layer mechanisms such as Differentiated Services or Integrated Services.

  • Signaling applications MUST be able to carry labels.
  • The ability to carry labels MUST be extensible to support various types and numbers of labels, because a single binary value is not enough given the labeling standards that exist.
  • Signaling labels SHOULD map to the emergency labels used in other telephony networks such as the PSTN, so a call over a hybrid path can carry its labels end to end with translation at the boundaries. With no mapping, signaling reverts to a default service, presumably the one for the general public.
  • Application layer capabilities MUST NOT preclude application layer accounting, which is useful for billing and for tracking down abuse.
  • Gateways and stateful proxies that recognise ETS labels MUST be able to support a 'best available' service, probably better than best effort.

For best available service, the focus SHOULD be on the probability of forwarding packets. That probability may reach 100% depending on local policy for the label, and local policy MUST decide whether better than best effort applies to a given label. Being able to support it does not mean the mechanism is expected to be activated, and the RFC does not define how it is realised.
sections.eli5: The phone system must be able to attach a flag to an urgent call, understand different kinds of flags, and give flagged calls a better chance of getting through. How exactly is left for someone else to work out.

sections.title: Open Issues: Alternate Paths and Best Available Service
sections.content:
Section 4 lists issues for anyone designing solutions. It is not a list of requirements. The first is alternate paths. Experience with the Government Emergency Telecommunications Service (GETS) over the PSTN showed that alternate paths to a destination help emergency calls. On the Internet this may be harder and of more limited benefit: the PSTN fixes a path during call setup, while the Internet uses dynamic routing and has no concept of a call or call setup, even though IP telephony applications may be aware of calls.

The second is how far best available service reaches. Here its scope is limited to the application layer and the flows that pass through it. Support may be direct for the flow carrying the label, or indirect, for example when labels in signaling messages affect the matching data flows. How support is realised, and how effective it is, are outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: On the old phone network a call gets one fixed road, so you can plan a backup road. On the Internet every little packet picks its own road, which makes that idea trickier.

sections.title: Security Expectations for Labels
sections.content:
Only authorized users or operators SHOULD be able to create non-ordinary labels, meaning labels that may alter the default best effort service. Labels SHOULD come with mechanisms for strong end-to-end integrity while they travel through telephony systems.

Where operators are expected to act on labels, they SHOULD be able to authenticate the label on a received message. This is meant to prevent theft of service and reduce the risk of denial of service, for example by unauthorized users consuming limited resources. The general security discussion in RFC 3689 also applies.
sections.eli5: If anyone could stamp URGENT on their call, the stamp would be useless. So only the right people should be able to use it, and the stamp must not be forgeable on the way.
